newsitem.title: INDIA: Gold-Indian dealers seek tax relief.
newsitem.headline: Gold-Indian dealers seek tax relief.

text.p: Indian bullion dealers have called for fiscal relief and the removal of restrictions on expatriates bringing in gold, a spokesman for their organisation said on Monday.

Bombay Bullion Association president Makhan Lal Damani said he had suggested these changes in a memorandum to the government on the fiscal budget for 1997/98 (April/March), which is to be presented on February 28 in parliament.
"These measures will help gold trade in India, especially when international prices are at a low ebb," Damani told Reuters.
Gold prices in international markets touched a low of around $345 last week, the lowest since September 1993.

He said the bullion trade had suggested that expatriate Indians be allowed to bring in 10 kg of gold at any time without restrictions. At present they are allowed to bring in 10 kg once every six months subject to duty.
"This will further improve the flow of gold now that the prices have fallen to attractive levels," Damani said.
He said the introduction of gold cerificates to tap private holdings and the exemption of investments in gold from wealth tax are among other measures suggested by the association.
"Gold bonds will help the government tap private holdings for productive use while investment in gold can curb money supply and subsequently curb inflation," he said.
India, the world's largest consumer of gold, has an estimated 9,000 tonnes of gold in the form of private holdings, comprising mainly family heirlooms and jewellery given as part of dowries.
Damani said India's demand in the near term would depend on world prices and traditional wedding season buying across the country.
"Demand will be good because of low prices, which in turn will be dictated by global trends," he said.
In the week to Monday, the price of gold (24 carats) fell 95 rupees per 10 grammes to 4,835 rupees on Bombay's bullion market.

In Dubai, the Gulf re-export centre for gold, low world prices triggered strong demand as Indian sub-continent buyers prepared to celebrate Eid al-Fitr next week, at the end of the fasting month of Ramadan, dealers said on Sunday.
The Eid al-Fitr holiday, which is expected on February 10, is usually marked by the exchange of gifts, often jewellery or bullion.

"Demand is extremely good at the moment...Demand has gone up because of the low price so no one wants to miss the train. (Ramadan) demand is stronger than last year when prices were higher," one Dubai-based trader said.
The bullion market in Karachi, Pakistan's main commercial city, was closed on Monday as the country went to the polls to elect a national parliament.
GOLD PRICES 24 CARATS PER 10 GRAMS IN U.S. DOLLARS
(Conversion $=35.85 Indian rupees 40.22 Pakistani rupees and 3.67 UAE Dirhams)
* Bombay prices February 03/January 27, Karachi and Dubai February 2/January 26
